questions.q: Why does this lesson argue a FinOps tagging taxonomy from course 10 needs to be enforced at the landing zone rather than just documented as a best practice?
options: Documentation is technically impossible to use for tagging rules
If tagging is only recommended, resources get tagged inconsistently or not at all, and cost reports built on that data become wrong in ways that are hard to notice
Enforcement is only needed in AWS, never in Azure
A wiki page automatically applies tags to new resources
questions.explain: A taxonomy that's merely recommended produces inconsistent or missing tags, which silently corrupts any cost report built on top of that tag data.

questions.q: What does an Azure Policy assignment using the 'Require a tag on resources' definition with a Deny effect actually do?
options: It only warns after the resource has already been created
It blocks a resource from being created at all if the required tag is missing
It automatically renames the tag to a standard value
It applies only to resource groups, never to individual resources
questions.explain: A Deny effect stops the deployment at creation time if the required tag is missing, instead of letting an untagged resource get created and surfacing the problem later in a cost report.

questions.q: On AWS, what is the role of a tag policy versus an SCP using the aws:RequestTag condition key?
options: A tag policy is preventive and an SCP is purely detective — the opposite of what this lesson describes
They do the exact same thing and either one alone is sufficient
A tag policy defines allowed keys/values and reports non-compliant resources (detective), while an SCP with aws:RequestTag can deny the creation call outright (preventive)
Tag policies and SCPs can only be used in separate, unrelated AWS accounts
questions.explain: The AWS pattern mirrors Azure's: the SCP is the preventive Deny-at-creation control, and the tag policy is the ongoing detective compliance report.

questions.q: Why does requiring that a tag merely be *present* fail to solve the whole cost-allocation problem?
options: A present-but-free-text tag can produce inconsistent values like 'platform-team' vs 'Platform Team', which splits the same team's spend across multiple report rows
Presence requirements make cost reporting impossible entirely
Azure Policy cannot check whether a tag is present, only its value
Free-text tags are always rejected automatically by cloud providers
questions.explain: Without a constrained set of allowed values, a required-but-free-text tag still produces inconsistent values that undercount real spend when a cost dashboard groups by it.

questions.q: According to this lesson, how should a change to the tagging schema itself (adding a required key, renaming an allowed value) be handled?
options: As a quiet Slack message asking teams to start using the new tag going forward
It never needs to change once the taxonomy is first defined
As an architecture change reviewed in a pull request, the same way a network change would be, since policy and reporting both depend on it
Only finance needs to be informed, since it has no effect on resource creation
questions.explain: Because enforcement policy and chargeback/showback reporting both depend on the schema, a schema change has real consequences across every team under that scope and deserves the same reviewed-change process as any other governed infrastructure.
